variants.title: Define the space
variants.context: Cosine compares direction; inner product rewards direction and magnitude; Euclidean ranks by straight-line distance. Version the embedding model, preprocessing, dimension, type, normalization, metric, metadata schema, and deletion semantics as one unit; use a shadow index and reversible traffic shift for changes.
variants.prompt: Vectors are normalized to unit length. How do cosine and inner-product rankings relate?
options: They rank the same way, because magnitude no longer varies between vectors.
They stay unrelated, because inner product still rewards larger magnitudes.
Cosine turns into a magnitude comparison, so it stops ranking by direction.
optionFeedback: Unit vectors leave direction as the only difference, so the orderings agree.
Normalization removes the magnitude difference that made the two diverge.
Cosine compares direction by definition, and unit length removes magnitude rather than adding it.
variants.explanation: If vectors are normalized, cosine and inner-product ranking are closely related.

variants.title: Define the space
variants.context: Cosine compares direction; inner product rewards direction and magnitude; Euclidean ranks by straight-line distance. Version the embedding model, preprocessing, dimension, type, normalization, metric, metadata schema, and deletion semantics as one unit; use a shadow index and reversible traffic shift for changes.
variants.prompt: The distance metric is changed in deployment configuration but the index version is unchanged. What is the risk?
options: Search gets faster, because the new metric skips the normalization step.
Stored scores and neighbors no longer match the recorded contract.
There is no risk, since the metric is only a query-time setting.
optionFeedback: Metric choice changes the ranking, and it is not a normalization shortcut.
The metric is part of the space definition, so version it with the index.
The metric defines the space the stored vectors were built for, not just the query.
variants.hint: Where should the metric be recorded?
variants.explanation: Record the contract in the collection or index version.

variants.title: Define the space
variants.context: Cosine compares direction; inner product rewards direction and magnitude; Euclidean ranks by straight-line distance. Version the embedding model, preprocessing, dimension, type, normalization, metric, metadata schema, and deletion semantics as one unit; use a shadow index and reversible traffic shift for changes.
variants.prompt: The embedding model is upgraded. What is the safe rollout?
options: Build a shadow index and shift traffic onto it in reversible steps.
Overwrite vectors with the new model as documents are next touched.
Point the embedding service at the new model and keep serving the same index.
optionFeedback: Changing any contract field can require a new index, so keep the old one intact.
Lazy overwrite mixes two embedding spaces in one index, and scores stop comparing.
The existing index holds old-model vectors, so new query vectors land in the wrong space.
variants.hint: Can old and new vectors share one space?
variants.explanation: Use a shadow index and a reversible traffic shift.

variants.title: Choose the index
variants.context: Choose an index from the workload: exact flat search for ground truth and small corpora; HNSW for high-recall in-memory search; IVF with product quantization to partition and compress; disk-oriented graphs for larger-than-memory corpora. Benchmark the whole recall-latency curve.
variants.prompt: You need exact top-k ground truth for evaluation over 50,000 vectors. Which index?
options: Product quantization.
Exact flat search.
HNSW.
optionFeedback: Compression loses exactness.
Exact search scores every eligible vector and is practical at this size.
ANN accepts misses.
variants.explanation: Keep exact search available for evaluation samples.

variants.title: Choose the index
variants.context: Choose an index from the workload: exact flat search for ground truth and small corpora; HNSW for high-recall in-memory search; IVF with product quantization to partition and compress; disk-oriented graphs for larger-than-memory corpora. Benchmark the whole recall-latency curve.
variants.prompt: A 50-million-vector corpus must serve high recall from memory with tunable latency. Which index?
options: Exact flat search, which guarantees recall at every corpus size.
No index at all, scanning the raw vectors on a wider machine.
HNSW, tuning query-time search effort for the recall-latency point.
optionFeedback: Exact scan of 50 million vectors per query is too slow for a serving path.
Scanning without an index is the same exact search, and hardware does not close that gap.
Graph traversal gives high recall with controllable query-time effort.
variants.hint: Which family trades effort for recall in memory?
variants.explanation: Query-time search effort controls the operating point.

variants.title: Choose the index
variants.context: Choose an index from the workload: exact flat search for ground truth and small corpora; HNSW for high-recall in-memory search; IVF with product quantization to partition and compress; disk-oriented graphs for larger-than-memory corpora. Benchmark the whole recall-latency curve.
variants.prompt: The corpus exceeds memory. Which family fits, and what enters the latency model?
options: Exact search, since scanning from disk avoids the index build cost.
A disk-oriented graph, so storage layout and IO enter the latency model.
In-memory HNSW, with the operating system paging the graph as needed.
optionFeedback: Exact search from disk is slower still, and it reads far more data per query.
Compact routing stays in memory while candidate neighborhoods live on SSD.
Paging a proximity graph turns every hop into an unpredictable disk read.
variants.explanation: Include SSD footprint and restart recovery in benchmarks.

variants.title: Do the filter math
variants.context: Fixed post-filtering fails on selective predicates: retrieve 40 global candidates with 5% eligible and about two survive. Filter during candidate generation, adapt search depth with a hard bound, or route to exact search over the eligible set.
variants.prompt: A service retrieves 40 global candidates and only 5% are eligible for this tenant. About how many candidates survive?
variants.hint: Multiply candidates by the eligible fraction.
variants.explanation: 40 × 0.05 = 2 candidates on average; a top-10 request cannot be repaired by reranking two results.

variants.title: Do the filter math
variants.context: Fixed post-filtering fails on selective predicates: retrieve 40 global candidates with 5% eligible and about two survive. Filter during candidate generation, adapt search depth with a hard bound, or route to exact search over the eligible set.
variants.prompt: To expect 10 eligible results at 5% eligibility with fixed post-filtering, how many global candidates would you need?
variants.hint: Divide the target by the eligible fraction.
variants.explanation: 10 ÷ 0.05 = 200 global candidates, which risks crossing the isolation boundary; filter during candidate generation instead.

variants.title: Do the filter math
variants.context: Fixed post-filtering fails on selective predicates: retrieve 40 global candidates with 5% eligible and about two survive. Filter during candidate generation, adapt search depth with a hard bound, or route to exact search over the eligible set.
variants.prompt: Exact search returns the true top 10. The ANN index returns 8 of them. What is recall@10, in percent?
variants.hint: Divide found true neighbors by k.

variants.title: Assign the owner
variants.context: Stage ownership: the embedding service owns tokenization, preprocessing, dimensions, normalization, and model version; the write path owns point identity, version ordering, tombstones, and retry deduplication; the index owns candidate generation and which write sequence is searchable; the query service owns authorization, deadline, search effort, fallback, and reranking. Empty results are a valid authorization outcome.
variants.prompt: A tenant’s filtered search returns nothing. What should the query service do?
options: Treat the empty result as a valid authorization outcome and return it.
Retry the search without the tenant filter so the result set is not empty.
Enlarge the global candidate set until something appears.
optionFeedback: Empty is a legitimate answer when the tenant owns no matching evidence.
Dropping the filter crosses the isolation boundary and can return another tenant's records.
Enlarging candidates past the filter risks surfacing unauthorized content.
variants.hint: What would removing the filter expose?
variants.explanation: Treat empty results as valid; never enlarge candidates past the isolation boundary.

variants.title: Assign the owner
variants.context: Stage ownership: the embedding service owns tokenization, preprocessing, dimensions, normalization, and model version; the write path owns point identity, version ordering, tombstones, and retry deduplication; the index owns candidate generation and which write sequence is searchable; the query service owns authorization, deadline, search effort, fallback, and reranking. Empty results are a valid authorization outcome.
variants.prompt: Duplicate writes arrive after a retry. Which stage prevents duplicate points?
options: The write path, via stable point identity and retry deduplication.
The embedding service, which returns the same vector for the same text.
The reranker, which collapses near-identical results before they return.
optionFeedback: Identity, ordering, and deduplication belong to the write path.
Identical vectors still land as two separate points without a stable ID.
Reranking runs at query time, long after both duplicates were stored.
variants.explanation: The write path owns stable identity, version ordering, tombstones, and retry deduplication.

variants.title: Assign the owner
variants.context: Stage ownership: the embedding service owns tokenization, preprocessing, dimensions, normalization, and model version; the write path owns point identity, version ordering, tombstones, and retry deduplication; the index owns candidate generation and which write sequence is searchable; the query service owns authorization, deadline, search effort, fallback, and reranking. Empty results are a valid authorization outcome.
variants.prompt: A query is served against a write that is not yet searchable. Who publishes which writes are searchable?
options: The embedding service, which stamps each vector with its model version.
The index, which publishes the searchable write sequence as a checkpoint.
The query service, which decides how long to wait for fresh writes.
optionFeedback: Model version is an embedding concern and says nothing about freshness.
The index owns candidate generation and the checkpoint that publishes it.
The query service consumes that checkpoint rather than producing it.
variants.hint: Which stage knows the searchable checkpoint?
variants.explanation: Return index checkpoints so freshness is reproducible.
